reports.name: Shohei Ohtani
reports.published_report: Ohtani is the only player in baseball you have to scout twice — and both reads come back elite. On the hitting side, the contact quality is almost absurd: .416 xwOBA, 93.8 mph average exit velocity, and a 16.6% barrel rate all sit at 96th percentile or better, and a 15.4% walk rate rounds out a profile that makes .399 OBP look like a floor, not a ceiling. The one honest wrinkle is a 28.3% whiff rate — that's 31st percentile — but when you're barreling the ball at this rate and taking walks at that clip, pitchers are stuck choosing their poison. On the mound, a 98.0 mph fastball, 2485 rpm spin, and 30.9% whiff rate combine for a 2.68 xERA that would anchor a rotation; ValuCast projects him to .286/.399/.552 with 39 home runs as a DH, and the Statcast profile says that's not optimistic.

reports.name: James Wood
reports.published_report: James Wood is a 23-year-old with elite raw power and a strike-zone approach that's genuinely unusual for his age — 15.8% walks against a 23.4% chase rate tell you he's hunting his pitch, not flailing. The contact piece is the honest question: a 32.2% whiff rate and 30.6% strikeout rate sit in the bottom tier of the league, and that gap between his .588 xSLG (99th percentile) and his 75th-percentile xBA is the whole story — when he connects, it's damage, but he misses a lot. ValuCast projects him at .260/.375/.496 with 36 home runs and 22 steals over 730 plate appearances, which is a middle-of-the-order profile if the strikeout rate stabilizes even modestly. The bat speed and barrel numbers — 95.2 mph average exit velo, 23.0% barrel rate, both maxing the scale — suggest the power is real and durable; the question is simply how often he gets to it.

The one real thing standing between him and stardom is a 36.5% whiff rate that checks in at the 3rd percentile — he draws walks at a historic clip because he knows the zone, but when he does swing at breaking stuff he can be put away, and that 30.6% strikeout rate is the number that will get tested as he sees better scouting. reports.name: William Contreras
reports.published_report: William Contreras is one of the cleaner hitters in the National League — a catcher who makes consistent hard contact and almost never strikes out. His 13.2% K rate and 19.0% whiff rate both sit in the 89th and 80th percentiles respectively, and his xBA of .285 (89th percentile) tells you the .286 projection isn't a fluke or a lucky BABIP story — he's genuinely squaring the ball up. The xSLG of .466 (80th percentile) running ahead of his projected .432 SLG suggests there's a little more thump in the bat than the counting stats will show, and ValuCast's projection of 19 HR with a .362 OBP over 645 PA reflects a dependable everyday presence, not a boom-or-bust gamble. The one real ceiling limiter here isn't the bat — it's the legs; a sprint speed of 25.4 ft/s puts him in the 11th percentile, so the floor on his value is tied almost entirely to what he gives you behind the plate.

reports.name: Riley Greene
reports.published_report: Riley Greene is a plus hitter with legitimate thump — the contact quality metrics here are what you'd build an offensive corner outfielder around. His 92.1 mph average exit velocity (89th percentile), 14.0% barrel rate (87th), and 51.6% hard-hit rate (93rd) tell you the raw damage is real, and a 12.3% BB rate (84th percentile) says he earns his way on base rather than just hoping to put it in play. The one thing that decides his ceiling is the strikeout problem: a 29.9% whiff rate (22nd percentile) and 26.9% K% (20th percentile) are the friction in the machine — he makes elite contact when he connects, but he misses too often for the batting average to reflect the underlying quality, which is exactly why the ValuCast projection sits at .276/.361/.454 with 23 home runs instead of something louder. Fix the whiff rate even partially and you're talking about a legitimate middle-of-the-order bat; leave it where it is and you've got a very good player carrying an exploitable hole.

reports.name: Cooper Pratt
reports.published_report: Cooper Pratt is a 21-year-old shortstop whose future hinges almost entirely on whether he can hit enough to stay in a lineup — and right now, the answer is probably not. The ValuCast projection over 289 PA has him at .220/.302/.312 with a .614 OPS, which is fringe-roster production at best for a corner bat and outright replacement-level if you're asking him to carry a premium defensive position. What keeps him interesting is the sprint speed — 79th percentile at 28.4 ft/s — which explains the 13 projected steals and gives him a real non-bat tool; a guy who can run like that and play shortstop has a job description, it just requires the bat to be functional. Four home runs in 289 trips tells you the power isn't coming to bail him out, so the question is whether he develops enough contact and on-base ability to profile as a speedy utility piece. Medium confidence from ValuCast here, and honestly that feels right for a 21-year-old with a thin MLB track record and a profile that lives or dies by a skill — hitting — that isn't there yet.

reports.name: Rafael Devers
reports.published_report: Rafael Devers is a pure raw-power hitter whose bat speed and contact quality are genuinely elite — 92.2 mph average exit velocity and a 51.3% hard-hit rate put him in the 90th and 93rd percentiles, respectively — but the swing-and-miss is the real anchor on his value. A 29.9% whiff rate and 29.2% K% land him in the bottom quarter of the league on both, and that's why his xBA sits at .225 despite all that loudness. The projection (.241/.319/.452, 28 HR in 675 PA) reflects exactly that tension: a middle-of-the-order power threat who gives back a chunk of his damage through strikeouts and a below-average walk rate of 8.1%. Until the contact rate improves, the ceiling on his slash line is essentially capped by how often pitchers can get him to expand.

reports.name: Isaac Paredes
reports.published_report: Isaac Paredes is a pure-contact-discipline bat with real power limitations — a guy who earns his way on base through a 17.3% whiff rate and 9.7% BB% rather than anything happening at contact. The Statcast profile is blunt about it: 86.9 mph average exit velocity and 29.9% hard-hit rate sit at the bottom of the league, and his xSLG of .362 signals that the 24 projected home runs are running a bit ahead of what the underlying contact quality actually supports. The walk rate and bat-to-ball skills are legitimate, though — they're what prop the projection to a .346 OBP and keep him useful in a lineup even when the ball isn't jumping off the bat. The real question for Paredes is whether the discipline-over-thump profile holds up enough in Houston to justify everyday third-base at-bats, because there's no carrying tool here beyond the strike zone.
